mcqs.question: Why did Lambda architecture emerge, historically?
options: Batch engines could not process large volumes of data at all
Regulatory requirements mandated running two separate pipelines
Streaming engines of the time were less mature for correctness-critical results, so batch handled correctness while streaming handled freshness
Lambda was designed to reduce infrastructure cost compared to a single pipeline
mcqs.explanation: Lambda's dual-pipeline design was a pragmatic response to streaming engines being newer and less trusted for correctness at the time, letting batch provide the authoritative recomputation while streaming gave fast approximate results. It wasn't a regulatory mandate, batch engines could process large volumes fine, and running two pipelines adds cost rather than reducing it.

mcqs.question: A team's Lambda batch layer and speed layer start producing disagreeing numbers for the same period. What's the most likely underlying cause?
options: This is expected Lambda behavior and requires no investigation
The raw input data was corrupted
Lambda architectures cannot produce consistent results by design
The batch and streaming codebases implementing the same business logic have drifted apart after a change was made to one but not the other
mcqs.explanation: Because Lambda maintains the same logic in two separate codebases, a fix or change applied to one but not the other is the classic cause of a genuine, unintended disagreement, distinct from the expected fast-then-corrected pattern. It isn't expected behavior needing no investigation, and this is a maintenance risk, not a fundamental design flaw or evidence of data corruption.

mcqs.question: A team wants to adopt Kappa architecture but their event log only retains 7 days of history, while they sometimes need to reprocess a year of data. What's the implication?
options: Kappa's core replay mechanism won't work as designed, since there isn't enough retained history to replay from
This has no effect since Kappa doesn't rely on log retention
The streaming engine will automatically extend retention as needed
This only matters for Lambda architectures, not Kappa
mcqs.explanation: Kappa's entire reprocessing mechanism depends on being able to replay far enough back in the log — with only 7 days retained, a year-long reprocessing need simply has no raw data to replay from. Log retention is a core Kappa precondition, not something engines extend automatically, and it's specifically a Kappa concern since Lambda's batch layer doesn't depend on stream replay at all.

mcqs.question: According to the comparison, when is Lambda still the more defensible choice over Kappa today?
options: When replay volume/duration makes Kappa's retention requirement impractical, or existing batch infrastructure investment doesn't yet justify migration
Lambda is never justified anymore now that streaming engines have matured
Lambda is always superior regardless of streaming engine maturity
Only when the team has no streaming engine available at all
mcqs.explanation: Lambda remains genuinely justified specifically when Kappa's replay precondition can't practically be met, or when deep existing batch investment makes a full migration premature — not as a blanket rule in either direction. It isn't universally obsolete nor universally superior, and Lambda actually requires a streaming engine for its speed layer, so 'no streaming engine at all' wouldn't support Lambda either.

mcqs.question: A framework advertises a unified batch-and-streaming API. What should you verify before assuming it fully escapes the Lambda-vs-Kappa trade-off?
options: Nothing — a unified API automatically guarantees shared semantics
That the batch and streaming modes genuinely share semantics under the shared execution engine, not just a similar-looking API over two different engines
That the framework only supports batch processing
That the framework has no relationship to either Lambda or Kappa concepts
mcqs.explanation: A similar API surface doesn't guarantee the two modes actually execute with the same underlying semantics — verifying that is what determines whether you've genuinely avoided the drift-and-retention trade-offs, or just hidden them behind one API. This capability directly addresses both Lambda's drift problem and Kappa's retention precondition, so it's very much related to both, and it must support both batch and streaming to be relevant here at all.

mcqs.question: A fintech team's event log retains only 30 days, but regulators require a year of replay-capable auditability, and their streaming engine is new to the team. Which architecture does the worked example favor?
options: Kappa, since it always produces more auditable results than Lambda
Neither architecture applies to financial ledger reconciliation
Kappa, because streaming engines are inherently more trustworthy for financial data
Lambda, since the retention shortfall and unproven streaming engine make Kappa's preconditions unmet, making the proven batch layer the safer choice for the audited number
mcqs.explanation: With retention short of the regulatory requirement and an unproven streaming engine, Kappa's two preconditions aren't met, so Lambda's proven batch layer producing the audited number is the safer call — exactly the reasoning the worked example walks through. Auditability isn't automatically better under either architecture; it depends on whether the specific preconditions for reliability are actually satisfied, and both architectures apply to reconciliation scenarios like this one.
